name: Distributed Cache (Redis Cluster)
description: Design a distributed caching layer using Redis Cluster. Covers consistent hashing, cache-aside/write-through patterns, cluster topology, replication, and failover.

learnSteps.title: Cache-Aside (Lazy Loading) Pattern
learnSteps.description: The Application Server first checks Redis for the requested key. On a cache hit (~95%), data is returned in under 1ms. On a cache miss, the server queries PostgreSQL, writes the result into Redis with a TTL, and returns it. This lazy-loading approach ensures only actively-accessed data occupies cache memory. The tradeoff is that the first request for any key incurs a full DB round-trip.

learnSteps.title: Consistent Hashing and Slot Assignment
learnSteps.description: Redis Cluster partitions the keyspace into 16,384 hash slots distributed across 3 master shards. Each key is hashed (CRC16) to determine its slot and thus its shard. When a node is added or removed, only the slots migrating to/from that node are affected, minimizing cache invalidation. Clients use cluster-aware drivers that maintain a slot-to-node mapping and redirect automatically on MOVED responses.

learnSteps.title: Replication and Automatic Failover
learnSteps.description: Each of the 3 master shards has 1 replica, forming a 6-node cluster. Replicas asynchronously replicate from their master. If a master fails, the cluster's gossip protocol detects it within seconds, and the replica is promoted to master (automatic failover). During failover, writes to that shard's slots may fail briefly, so the application retries with exponential backoff. Read replicas can serve stale reads for lower latency in read-heavy workloads.

learnSteps.title: Cache Invalidation Strategies
learnSteps.description: Three common strategies: (1) TTL-based expiry -- keys expire after a fixed time, trading freshness for simplicity. (2) Write-through -- on every DB write, the app also updates Redis, keeping cache consistent but adding write latency. (3) Event-driven invalidation -- DB changes emit events that trigger cache deletes, using eventual consistency. Choosing the right strategy depends on how stale data tolerance vs write complexity trade off for each use case.

chaosScenarios.name: Master Shard Failure
chaosScenarios.description: One of the 3 Redis master nodes crashes, taking its ~5,461 hash slots offline until the replica is promoted
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Gossip marks the master failed within cluster-node-timeout (~5-15s) and the replica promotes automatically. Reads and writes to that shard's slots error briefly; cluster-aware clients refresh slot maps on MOVED responses. Writes still in async replication flight at crash time are lost.
mitigationSteps: Application retries with exponential backoff through the promotion window
Clients refresh slot-to-node topology on MOVED/CLUSTERDOWN errors
Provision a replacement node and attach it as replica of the promoted master
Audit the lost-write window — the cache must never be the source of truth

chaosScenarios.name: Cache Avalanche on Synchronized TTL Expiry
chaosScenarios.description: A large keyset written at the same moment (e.g., after a deploy or bulk warm) expires together at the 3600s TTL, collapsing the hit rate
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: Hit rate drops from ~95% toward zero for the affected keyset; miss traffic multiplies database queries 10-20x and the 500-connection PostgreSQL pool saturates. Request latency climbs from ~20ms to seconds as queries queue behind the pool.
mitigationSteps: Add random jitter (±10%) to TTLs on re-population
Coalesce concurrent misses per key (singleflight) at the application layer
Rate-limit the miss path to protect the database pool
Warm the hottest keys from access logs before lifting limits

chaosScenarios.name: Split-Brain Network Partition
chaosScenarios.description: A partition isolates one master from the cluster majority while some application servers can still reach it
chaosScenarios.expectedBehavior: The majority side promotes the replica; the isolated master keeps accepting writes until it detects the partition and demotes itself. Writes accepted on the minority side during that window are discarded on heal — a silent lost-update anomaly.
mitigationSteps: Tune cluster-node-timeout to bound the dirty-write window
Treat cache contents as reconstructable, never durable state
Verify full slot coverage and replica topology after the partition heals
Invalidate keys written during the partition window where correctness matters

bottleneckProgression.description: At ~95% hit rate the miss traffic plus write-backs already hold hundreds of PostgreSQL connections; any hit-rate dip saturates the 500-connection pool
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Add PgBouncer pooling, jitter TTLs, coalesce duplicate miss queries

bottleneckProgression.description: 10 application instances at ~15ms processing per request run out of CPU headroom
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Scale out instances, pipeline Redis commands, trim per-request serialization

bottleneckProgression.description: Hot-key skew drives one shard's single-threaded Redis command loop to 100% while the other shards idle
bottleneckProgression.resolution: Reshard slots, serve hot keys from replicas or a client-side near cache, split jumbo keys

expectedIssues.title: Hot Key Skew
expectedIssues.description: A handful of celebrity keys hash to a single slot, pinning load on one shard no matter how many shards exist
expectedIssues.mitigation: Client-side near cache for top-N keys, read hot keys from replicas, replicate hot keys under derived names

expectedIssues.title: Thundering Herd on Popular Key Expiry
expectedIssues.description: When a popular key expires, every app instance misses simultaneously and all issue the same database query
expectedIssues.mitigation: Singleflight request coalescing, probabilistic early refresh before TTL, mutex-guarded rebuild

expectedIssues.title: Lost Writes After Failover
expectedIssues.description: Async replication means a promoted replica can be missing the final moments of writes; readers silently see older values
expectedIssues.mitigation: Design the cache as disposable, use WAIT for rare critical writes, fall back to DB reads when in doubt

expectedIssues.title: Silent Hit-Rate Decay From LRU Eviction
expectedIssues.description: When the working set outgrows 128GB, allkeys-lru evicts warm keys and the hit rate degrades gradually with no hard failure to alert on
expectedIssues.mitigation: Alert on evicted_keys rate and hit-rate trend, add shards before memory pressure, audit TTLs on bulky keysets

expectedIssues.title: Cache-Aside Read/Write Race
expectedIssues.description: A read-miss racing a concurrent database update can repopulate the cache with the pre-update value, pinning stale data until TTL expiry
expectedIssues.mitigation: Delete (not update) cache entries on write, keep TTLs short for mutable data, version keys

metrics.name: cache_hit_rate
metrics.description: Fraction of reads served from Redis

metrics.name: evicted_keys_total
metrics.description: Keys evicted by allkeys-lru under memory pressure

metrics.name: shard_cpu_utilization
metrics.description: Per-shard Redis main-thread CPU — the hot-key detector

metrics.name: db_pool_in_use
metrics.description: PostgreSQL connections consumed by miss traffic

metrics.name: request_latency
metrics.description: End-to-end request latency including the miss path

steps: Run CLUSTER INFO / CLUSTER NODES — confirm promotion finished and all 16,384 slots are covered
Check application error rates and confirm retries absorbed the promotion window
Provision a replacement node and attach it as replica of the promoted master
Review the async-replication lost-write window with owning teams
Capture the timeline for the postmortem
Determine whether the drop is expiry-driven (expired_keys spike) or eviction-driven (evicted_keys spike)
Enable miss-path rate limiting and request coalescing to protect PostgreSQL
Re-populate with jittered TTLs to break expiry synchronization
Warm the hottest keys from access logs
Lift limits once hit rate exceeds 90%
Identify oversized keysets with redis-cli --bigkeys and MEMORY USAGE sampling
Shorten TTLs or drop low-value keysets
Add a shard pair and rebalance slots during low traffic
Verify hit rate and eviction rate return to baseline

decisions.title: Cache-Aside as the Default Access Pattern
decisions.context: Read-heavy workload tolerant of brief staleness; cache memory is the scarce resource
decisions.decision: Lazy-load on miss with a 1-hour TTL; only the application writes to the cache
consequences: Only actively-read data occupies the 128GB of memory
First access to any key pays a full database round-trip
Staleness is bounded by TTL unless writes invalidate explicitly

decisions.title: Redis Cluster: 3 Shards × 1 Replica
decisions.context: The working set exceeds a single node and the layer needs automatic failover
decisions.decision: Partition 16,384 slots across 3 masters with one replica each; gossip-driven promotion on failure
consequences: Capacity and throughput scale by resharding slots
Multi-key operations restricted to keys in the same slot (hash tags)
Brief per-shard write unavailability during failover

tradeoffs.cost: Acknowledged writes can vanish on failover — the cache can never be the source of truth

tradeoffs.benefit: The database sees only ~5% of read traffic
tradeoffs.cost: Readers may see data up to an hour old unless writes invalidate

alternatives.name: Memcached Fleet
alternatives.description: Client-side consistent hashing over stateless Memcached nodes
alternatives.prosVsCons: Simpler and multithreaded per node, but no replication or failover — a node loss is a cold-start miss storm
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Built-in replication, automatic failover, and richer data types favor Redis Cluster

alternatives.name: Write-Through Cache
alternatives.description: Synchronously update the cache on every database write
alternatives.prosVsCons: Fresher data and fewer misses, but adds latency to every write and caches keys that may never be read
alternatives.whyNotChosen: The workload is read-heavy and tolerates TTL-bounded staleness

alternatives.name: Single Large Redis Instance + Replica
alternatives.description: One 128GB primary with a single replica instead of a sharded cluster
alternatives.prosVsCons: Simplest topology with no cross-slot limits, but full-sync and failover of 128GB is slow and one main thread caps throughput
alternatives.whyNotChosen: Sharding bounds the blast radius and scales single-threaded command processing horizontally
